description: Against the Silence is a NASA Space Apps team building AEGIS-MEDLINK, an offline AI-powered astronaut health monitoring and resilient medical communication system. Led by an MSc AI & Data Science student experienced in AI and distributed systems, we welcome teammates interested in medicine, biomedical engineering, aerospace, telecommunications, and UI/UX. Care Beyond Connectivity.
summary:
Astronauts on the way to Mars will spend long periods with no live link to Earth. A message can take up to 22 minutes to arrive, and blackouts can cut contact completely. If a crew member's heart rate or oxygen drops during that silence, nobody on the ground knows.

AEGIS-MEDLINK is built for those gaps. On board, AEGIS checks heart rate and blood oxygen against each astronaut's own normal levels. It uses simple rules and statistics, not an AI model, so every alert can be explained. It warns the crew straight away and asks how they feel.

Each event becomes a PulseBrief: a one-line headline, the context, and the full evidence. MEDLINK sends these over real delay-tolerant networking (BPv7). It holds them while the link is down and delivers them, headline first, as soon as the link returns. Nothing is lost.

Doctors on Earth get the full picture, even after a blackout, and the crew is never left alone with a medical problem.

All data in the demo is simulated. This is not a medical device.
details:
What it does

On the way to Mars, a message takes up to 22 minutes to reach Earth, and for about two weeks there can be no contact at all. AEGIS-MEDLINK makes sure a medical problem during that time is caught on board and still reaches Earth's doctors.

  • AEGIS runs on the spacecraft and doesn't need Earth. It checks heart rate and blood oxygen against each astronaut's own normal levels. It ignores exercise and loose sensors, and when something is wrong it says what it saw and what to do now.
  • PulseBrief packs each event into three layers; headline, context and evidence. In a short contact window, the headline goes first.
  • MEDLINK sends these over real delay-tolerant networking (BPv7). When the link drops, messages wait on board and are delivered once it's back. The doctors' reply returns the same way.

Benefits and impact

The crew gets help straight away, and doctors get the key facts first. In our test, 21 KB of briefs replaced 2.7 MB of raw data, and no event was lost across repeated blackouts. The same idea fits research stations, ships and remote clinics.

How we built it

We used Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, dtn7-rs, Next.js, React Three Fiber and Blender, along with NASA DONKI space-weather data, Deep Space Network station positions, and NASA imagery and 3D models. The checks use rules and statistics rather than an AI model, so every alert can be explained.

What we considered

We focused on trust, avoiding false alarms, low bandwidth and honesty. All crew data is simulated and labelled as such, and this is not a medical device.
